concepts.title: Multilabel classification
concepts.one_liner: Multilabel classification can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems.
concepts.content:
When the image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems (where $K$ is the number of classes).

In such a case, the function $f_\theta$ can be a neural network shared across all classes (@fig-class_architecture), and the output vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, of length $K$, is computed using a sigmoid nonlinearity for each output class. In this case the output can still be interpreted as the probability $\hat{y}_c = p_\theta(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, but without the constraint that the sum across classes is 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Multilabel classification addresses cases where images contain multiple classes simultaneously, requiring independent probability estimates per class.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multilabel classification treats each class as a binary problem.
- Outputs use sigmoid nonlinearities per class.
- Probabilities per class do not sum to one.

concepts.one_liner: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps: proposing candidate bounding boxes, classifying each proposed box, and postprocessing to remove redundant detections.

concepts.title: Selective search
concepts.one_liner: Selective search proposes an initial set of bounding boxes likely to contain objects, reducing computation by applying expensive classifiers only to promising regions.
concepts.content: The window scanning approach can be slow as the same classifier needs to be applied to tens of thousands of image patches. Selective search makes the process more efficient by proposing an initial set of bounding boxes that are good candidates to contain an object (@fig-selective_search_pipeline). This proposal mechanism is performed by a selection mechanism simpler than the object classifier. This approach was motivated by the strategy used by the visual system in which attention is first directed toward image regions likely to contain the target @wolfe2007, @TreismanGelade1980, @Koch_Ullman_1985. This first attentional mechanism is very fast but might be wrong. Therefore, a second, more accurate but also more expensive, processing stage is required in order to take a reliable decision. The advantage of this **cascade** of decisions is that the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations (the ones selected by the cheap attentional mechanism) dramatically reducing the overall computational cost.
concepts.motivation_md: Selective search speeds up object detection by focusing expensive classification only on promising image regions, inspired by human visual attention mechanisms.
concepts.recap_md:
- Window scanning is slow due to many image patches.
- Selective search proposes candidate bounding boxes efficiently.
- It uses a fast, simple selection before expensive classification, forming a cascade.

concepts.title: nonmaximum suppression
concepts.one_liner: Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) discards overlapping detections likely corresponding to the same object, outputting only one bounding box per instance.
concepts.content:
We use **nonmaximum suppression** (NMS) to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, so as to output only one bounding box for each instance present in the image.

The nonmaximum suppression algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, $S=\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$\, and outputs a smaller set removing overlapping bounding boxes. It is an iterative algorithm as follows: 
(1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set $S$ and add it to the final set $S^*$.
(2) Remove from $S$ the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold.
(3) Go to step 1 until $S$ is empty.
concepts.motivation_md: NMS resolves multiple overlapping detections of the same object by selecting the most confident bounding box and removing redundant ones, ensuring clean final outputs.

- NMS removes overlapping bounding boxes likely for the same object.
- It iteratively selects the highest confidence box and removes boxes with high IoU overlap.
- This outputs one bounding box per object instance.

concepts.one_liner: Supervised and unsupervised learning methods are state-of-the-art in motion estimation, but pursuing both learning and physically motivated algorithms is important.
concepts.content: Supervised and unsupervised learning-based methods are now the state-of-the-art in motion estimation. But an accurate solution is still missing. concepts.title: Geons

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Geons are a small set of geometric components used to represent objects by their arrangement and non-accidental attributes.
concepts.content: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing the object into a small set of geometric components (e.g., blocks, cylinders, cones, and so on.) that he called Geons. He derived 36 different Geons that we can discriminate visually. Geons are defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists in a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing objects as arrangements of simple geometric components (Geons) helps simplify and explain visual object recognition processes.

concepts.title: Compositionality

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), but visual compositionality is less strict than language compositionality.
concepts.content: One important aspect of his theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. Compositionality in the visual world is not as strong as the one found in language, where a fixed set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances (e.g., legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical). Geons are great to represent artificial objects (e.g., tables, cabinets, and phones) but fail when applied to represent stuff (e.g., grass, clouds, and water) or highly textured objects such as trees or food.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding compositionality explains how objects share components but also differ visually, highlighting limits of geometric component models like Geons for natural textures.

- Objects are composed of simpler elements called Geons.
- Visual compositionality is less strict than linguistic compositionality.
- Geons represent artificial objects well but struggle with natural textures.

concepts.title: Invariances

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Human object recognition is robust but not completely invariant to changes like viewpoint and illumination, with mental rotation explaining recognition across 3D rotations.
concepts.content:
Object recognition in humans seems to be quite robust to changes in viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, deformations, styles, and so on. However, perception is not completely invariant to those variables.

One well studied property of the human visual system is its invariance to image and 3D rotations. As we discussed in chapter @sec-bias_and_shift, studies in human visual perception have shown that objects are recognized faster when they appear in canonical poses. In a landmark study, Roger N. Shepard and Jaqueline Metzler @Shepard1971aa showed to participants pairs of drawings of three-dimensional objects (@fig-mental_rotation). The pair of drawings could show the same object with a mirror or the same object with an arbitrary 3D rotation. The task consisted in deciding if the two objects were identical (up to a 3D rotation) or mirror images of each other. During the experiment, they recorded the success rate and the reaction time (how long did participant took to answer). The result showed that participants had a reaction time proportional to the rotation angle between the two views. This supported the idea that participants were performing a mental rotation in order to compare both views. Whether humans actually perform mental rotations or not still remains controversial.

(see figure: Two figures related by a 3D rotation. Modified from @Shepard1971aa)
concepts.motivation_md: Studying invariances like viewpoint and illumination changes helps understand human object recognition robustness and the cognitive process of mental rotation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Human object recognition is robust but not fully invariant to changes.
- Recognition is faster for canonical poses.
- Mental rotation may explain recognition across 3D rotations.

concepts.title: cross-entropy loss
concepts.one_liner: The cross-entropy loss is differentiable and it is commonly used in image classification tasks.
concepts.content:
We get by just taking the negative log of the equation @eq-object_recognition-classification_likelihood, resulting in a total classification loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})
     = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)
$$

The cross-entropy loss is differentiable and it is commonly used in image classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-entropy loss provides a differentiable measure of classification error, enabling effective training of image classifiers by quantifying how well predicted probabilities match true labels.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cross-entropy loss is computed as the negative log of the classification likelihood.
- It sums over all classes and samples: $\mathcal{L}_{cls} = -\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^K y_c^{(t)} \log(\hat{y}_c^{(t)})$.
- It is differentiable and widely used in image classification tasks.

concepts.title: multiclass binary cross-entropy loss
concepts.one_liner: Taking the negative log of the likelihood gives the multiclass binary cross-entropy loss.
concepts.content:
$\hat{y}_c$ are computed using a sigmoid layer. Taking the negative log of the likelihood gives the **multiclass binary cross-entropy loss**:

$$\mathcal{L}_{cls}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})
     = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} y^{(t)}_c \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)
     + 
     (1-y^{(t)}_c) \log(1-\hat{y}^{(t)}_c)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Multiclass binary cross-entropy loss extends cross-entropy to multi-label classification by considering each class independently with sigmoid outputs, allowing multiple classes per example.
concepts.recap_md:
- Uses sigmoid outputs $\hat{y}_c$ for each class.
- Loss sums over all classes and samples with terms for positive and negative labels.
- Formula: $\mathcal{L}_{cls} = -\sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^K y_c^{(t)} \log(\hat{y}_c^{(t)}) + (1 - y_c^{(t)}) \log(1 - \hat{y}_c^{(t)})$.

concepts.title: top-1 performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction.
concepts.content:
Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set:

$$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T}
    \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)})
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Top-1 performance quantifies how often the classifier's highest confidence prediction matches the true label, providing a straightforward accuracy metric.
concepts.recap_md:
- Top-1 accuracy is the percentage of correct highest-score predictions.
- Computed as $\frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)})$.
- Reflects exact match between predicted and true class labels.

concepts.title: top-5 performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-5 performance is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions.
concepts.content: **Top-5** performance is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions. Top-5 is useful in settings where the labels might be ambiguous, or where multiple labels for one image might be possible. In the case of multiple labels, ideally, the test set should specify which labels are possible and evaluate only using those. The top-5 measure is less precise and it is used when the test set only contains one label despite that multiple labels might be correct.

concepts.title: Shortcomings
concepts.one_liner: Image classification has important limitations, including ambiguous class definitions and reliance on dataset biases.
concepts.content:
The task of image classification is plagued with issues. Although it is a useful task to measure progress in computer vision and machine learning, one has to be aware of its limitations when trying to use it to produce a meaningful description of a scene, or when developing a classifier for consumption in the real world.

One very important shortcoming of this task is that it assumes that we can actually answer unambiguously the question *does the image contains object c?* But what happens if class definitions are ambiguous or class boundaries are soft? Even in cases were we believe that the boundaries might be well defined, it is east to find images that will challenge our assumption, as shown in @fig-whatisacar.

[FIGURE:2f43ff582bf7c58e | A photograph of a car body shell in an assembly plant, held by a red robotic arm and a red 'SMART Cart' base. The car is incomplete, lacking windows, wheels, and interior components, illustrating the...]

[FIGURE:479c0a519751a2ba | A small yellow toy car with a strawberry decal on its roof and hood is parked in front of a cardboard castle. The image illustrates the ambiguity of object classification, questioning whether a toy...]

[FIGURE:aee6e4196eafb081 | A photograph of a white plate containing a slice of watermelon. A piece of the red fruit has been carved out into the silhouette of a car and placed separately on the plate, illustrating the...]

Which of these images contains a car? This is a simple question that does not have a simple answer.

Which of this images of @fig-whatisacar contains a car? A simple question that does not have a simple answer. The top three images contain cars, although with increasing difficulty. However, for the three images on the second row, it is not clear what the desired answer it is. We can clearly recognize the content of those images, but it feels as if using a single word for describing those images leaves too much ambiguity. Is a car under construction already a car? Is the toy car a car? And if we play with food and make a car out of watermelon, would that be a car? Probably not. But if a vision system classifies that shape as a car, would that be a mistake like any other?

Although it is not clearly stated in the problem definition, language plays a big role in object classification. The objects in @fig-object_recognition_pepper are easily recognizable to us, but if we ask the question "Is there a fruit in this picture?," the answer is a bit more complex than it might appear at first glance.

(see figure: A pepper is a fruit according to botanics, and it is a vegetable according to the culinary classification.)

What if the object is present in the scene but invisible in the image? What if there are infinite classes? In our formulation, $\hat {\bf y}$ is a vector of a fixed length. Therefore, we can only answer the question "is object class $c$ present in the image?" for a finite set of classes. What if we want to be able to answer an infinite set of questions? The next sections introduce more sophisticated formulations of object recognition that address some of these questions.

Is it possible to classify an image without localizing the object? How can we answer the question "Is object class $c$ present in the image?" without localizing the object? One possibility is that the function $f$ has learned to localize the object internally, but the information about the location is not being recorded in the output. Another possibility is that the function has learned to use other cues present in the image (biases in the dataset). As it is not trying to localize an object, the function $f$ will not get penalized if it uses shortcuts such as only recognizing one part of the object (e.g., such as the head of a dog, or car wheels), or if it makes use of contextual biases in the dataset (e.g., all images with grass and blue skies have horses, or all streets have cars) or detects unintended correlations between low-level image properties and the image content (e.g., all images of insects have a blurry background). As a consequence, image classification performance could mislead us into believing that the classifier works well and that it has learned a good representation of the object class it classifies.
concepts.motivation_md: Image classification is limited by ambiguous class definitions, soft boundaries, and dataset biases, which complicate meaningful scene description and real-world classifier deployment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Image classification assumes unambiguous class definitions, which is often unrealistic.
- Ambiguities arise from unclear boundaries and diverse object representations.
- Classifiers may rely on dataset biases or partial cues, misleading performance evaluation.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: The four different approaches we have described use a common set of building blocks: image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.
concepts.content:
@fig-pictorialsummary shows a pictorial summary of the different methods we have seen in this chapter to represent objects in images. The four different approaches we have described use a common set of building blocks: image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.

(see figure: A family of object recognition definitions.)

However, the representations we have described in this chapter feel very incomplete. If you are building a robot or an autonomous vehicle, such object representations are very hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object will need an accurate three-dimensional (3D) modeling of the object as well as an understanding of some of its physical properties in order to plan for the best grasping points. An autonomous vehicle will also need an accurate 3D description of the locations of objects in the world, together with a characterization of their dynamics. Therefore, object segmentation and classification only provide one part of the information needed.

The techniques we have described in this chapter rely on language to define what an object is (e.g., image tagging, captioning, etc.). What else can we do besides associating an object with a word? Here there are other questions that an object recognition system could try to answer:

- Is this piece of matter an object? could I find other instances that might belong to the same class or is it just a random arrangement of things with little chances of being found somewhere else?

- What is its 3D shape?

- Is it resting on the ground? How is it supported?

- What are its mechanical properties? Is it soft? Does it has parts? Is it rigid or deformable?

- How will it react to external actions? Can I grasp the object? How?

- What might this object be useful for? If I have to solve a task, can I use this object?

- Is it alive? Can I eat it?

- What is the physical process that created it? Is it artificial or natural?

- How did the object arrived to its current location?

- Is it stable? What will it do next?

Those are the questions that scientist would ask themselves when observing a new natural phenomena, and a computer vision system should behave as a scientist when confronted with a new visual stimuli. A system should formulate hypothesis about its visual input, devise experiments and perform interventions to answer them. One can rely on language to answer some or all of those questions, but language does not need to be the only internal representation used.
concepts.motivation_md: Object recognition methods use common building blocks but lack the full 3D and physical understanding needed for robotics or autonomous vehicles. This motivates deeper representations beyond language-based object tagging.
concepts.recap_md:
- Object recognition methods use image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression.
- Current methods provide incomplete representations for tasks like robotic grasping or autonomous driving.
- A vision system should answer deeper questions about 3D shape, physical properties, and dynamics beyond labeling.

concepts.title: Cascade of classifiers
concepts.one_liner: Cascade of classifiers divides the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy to efficiently localize objects in images.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduced the complexity of the search by dividing it into two steps: a first, fast, and cheap classification function that detects good candidate locations; and a second, slow, and expensive classification function capable of accurately classifying the object, applied only to a subset of all possible locations and scales. Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea further by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers with increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

The algorithm for the cascade of classifiers is:

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)

Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location, where each test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were inspired by the game "Twenty Questions".

In a cascade, computational power is allocated to image regions more likely to contain the target object, while flat or feature-poor regions are quickly rejected with minimal computation. The following figure from Fleuret and Geman illustrates how a cascaded classifier allocates computing power when trained to detect faces. The heat map intensity is proportional to the number of cascade levels applied at each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

It is interesting to note that the scanning window approach (Levels = 1) and the selective search procedure (Levels = 2) are special cases of this algorithm. The cascade of classifiers usually does not include a bounding box refinement stage since it starts with a full list of bounding boxes, but such a stage could be added to incorporate new transformations not available initially (e.g., rotations).
concepts.motivation_md: Localizing objects in images is challenging due to their small size and complex backgrounds. Cascade of classifiers efficiently allocates computation by quickly discarding unlikely regions and focusing resources on promising candidates, improving detection speed and accuracy.
concepts.recap_md:
- Cascade of classifiers uses a sequence of classifiers with increasing complexity to localize objects efficiently.
- Early classifiers quickly reject unlikely regions, saving computation.
- The approach generalizes scanning windows and selective search methods.

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The object localization loss combines classification and localization losses to train object detectors end-to-end by comparing predicted bounding boxes and labels with ground truth.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss accounts for two complementary tasks: classification and localization.

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label match the ground truth at that location?

- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

For each image, the object detector outputs a set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, where $B$ is likely larger than the number of ground truth bounding boxes in the training set. The first step is to associate each detection with a ground truth label, yielding $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. Predicted bounding boxes overlapping ground truth instances are optimized to improve predicted locations and labels. Remaining boxes that do not overlap ground truth are assigned to the background class ($\mathbf{y}_i=0$), and the model is optimized to reduce their predicted class scores.

This process is illustrated in the figure showing detector outputs compared with ground truth bounding boxes, where each detected box is assigned a ground truth label or background.

For classification loss, since each bounding box has one class, cross-entropy loss is used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = -  \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.

To measure localization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$, a common similarity measure is the Intersection over Union (IoU):

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

IoU ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical boxes). The localization loss is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1 - IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

IoU is translation and scale invariant and frequently used to evaluate object detectors. A simpler alternative is the L2 regression loss:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The L2 loss is translation invariant but not scale invariant and is larger for bigger bounding boxes. The next graph compares IoU loss and L2 regression loss for two square bounding boxes as a function of relative $x$-displacement.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

IoU loss becomes 1 when boxes do not overlap, resulting in no gradient information during backpropagation.

The overall loss combines classification and localization losses:

$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} 
     (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
$$

where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ zeroes the localization loss for bounding boxes not overlapping ground truth. The parameter $\lambda$ balances the relative strength of both losses. This loss enables end-to-end training of the detection algorithm, though localization and classification stages can also be trained independently.
concepts.motivation_md: Object detection requires both classifying what is in a bounding box and precisely localizing it. The object localization loss combines classification and localization terms to train detectors end-to-end, improving accuracy in both tasks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Object localization loss combines classification loss and localization loss.
- Classification loss uses cross-entropy to compare predicted and true labels.
- Localization loss often uses IoU or L2 regression to measure bounding box accuracy.

concepts.title: Precision-recall curve
concepts.one_liner: Precision-recall curve measures detection performance as a function of the decision threshold based on confidence scores.
concepts.content:
The **Precision-recall curve** measures the performance of a detection system as a function of the decision threshold. Each bounding box has a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, and a threshold $\beta$ is used to decide if an object is present at location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$.

Given threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$, and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$.

Precision is the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$

Precision alone does not account for missed detections. Recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances detected:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall range from 0 to 1, with high values indicating better performance. The following graph shows a precision-recall curve as a function of $\beta$.

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)
concepts.motivation_md: Precision-recall curves help evaluate detection algorithms by showing the trade-off between correctly detected objects and missed detections as the decision threshold varies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Precision-recall curve evaluates detection performance over thresholds.
- Precision = correct detections / total detections.
- Recall = correct detections / total ground truth instances.

concepts.title: stuff and objects
concepts.one_liner: Stuff refers to regions without well-defined boundaries, like grass or sky, contrasting with distinct object instances in images.
concepts.content:
It is useful to differentiate between **stuff** and **objects**. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky (discussed previously in textures). The distinction between stuff and objects is not very sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, like two trees in the left image below, or become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually, as shown in the right image. In cases with many instances, bounding boxes might not be appropriate; it is better to represent the region as "trees" than to try to detect each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)

concepts.title: semantic segmentation loss
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel over all classes and training examples.
concepts.content:
The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:

$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y})
     = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

where the sum is over all training examples, all classes, and all pixel locations.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation outputs pixel-level masks for each object instance, combining object detection and semantic segmentation.
concepts.content:
Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation by outputting a set of localized objects represented as pixel-level masks rather than bounding boxes, as shown in the figure below.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)

Unlike semantic segmentation, which aggregates pixels of the same class without distinguishing instances, instance segmentation outputs $K$ masks for $K$ objects of the same type, delineating overlapping objects.

One approach follows the object localization pipeline: after proposing and labeling bounding boxes, the cropped image within each box is fed to a binary semantic segmentation function that predicts, for each pixel in box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$, whether it belongs to the object or not, producing an instance mask for each box. This approach was introduced by He et al. The architecture is illustrated below.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)

Here, $f_0$ is a low-cost detector proposing regions likely to contain target object instances. The function $f_1$ performs classification and segmentation of the instance:

$$\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i,   \hat{\mathbf{s}}_i \right]= f_j(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ is the binary label confidence, and $\hat{s}_i \left[ n,m \right]$ is the instance segmentation mask.

The loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation losses:

$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$

The first classification loss corresponds to classifying the crop as containing the object or not; if present, the second term measures bounding box accuracy, and the third term measures whether the segmentation mask matches the ground truth instance segmentation. Parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ weight each loss.

This formulation can be extended to richer representations, such as regressing $u-v$ coordinates per pixel in an instance-centered frame, shape maps, or part segmentations.

- Combines object detection and semantic segmentation.
- Loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation terms.
